candidates.statement: This guidance is intended to convey to drug manufacturers FDA’s recommendations on how 17 certain drug products should be labeled regarding gluten, a matter of interest to individuals with 18 celiac disease. Some individuals with celiac disease have faced difficulty when trying to 19 determine whether specific drug products contain gluten. Confronted by uncertainty, some 20 patients may forego important medication rather than risk an adverse reaction to gluten. Thus, 21 even if gluten is not present at levels that would harm a typical individual with celiac disease, 22 that individual may be harmed through uncertainty and lack of information. 23
candidates.context: Celiac disease (also known as celiac sprue) is an immune-based reaction to dietary gluten that 25 primarily affects the small intestine in susceptible individuals; unmanaged celiac disease can lead 26 to serious health complications. Approximately 1 percent of the U.S. population has celiac 27 disease (Binder 2015). It is characterized by ongoing inflammation of part of the lining of the 28 small intestine that generally heals if foods containing gluten are excluded from the diet and 29 returns if they are reintroduced. At this time, the treatment for celiac disease is adherence to a 30 gluten-free diet. 31

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 61 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 62 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. candidates.context: 5 In this guidance, when we say added as an ingredient , we are referring to the intentional and purposeful addition of that ingredient. We are not referring to the introduction of wheat gluten, for example, as an unintended contaminant or impurity associated with an ingredient. Based on information available to us during our analyses for this guidance, we are aware of no oral drug products currently marketed in the United States that contain wheat gluten intentionally added as an inactive ingredient. Although the use of wheat gluten as an inactive ingredient in drug products does not generally 81 mean that the product will fail to satisfy applicable requirements for safety, we may question the 82 addition of wheat gluten to certain oral drug products on a case-by-case basis. candidates.statement: We are aware that some manufacturers have reported the direct addition of wheat flour to oral 118 drug products in the past—but only very rarely. We are not aware of an oral drug product 119 currently being marketed in the United States that contains wheat flour as an ingredient. As 120 discussed in section II.B of this guidance, any oral drug product that contains wheat flour as an 121 intentionally added ingredient should be labeled to indicate its presence. 122
candidates.context: The total protein content of wheat flour is generally 13 percent, with gluten representing part of 124 the total protein. 6 The amount of gluten present in an oral drug product to which wheat flour has 125 been added as an ingredient would depend on how much wheat flour is used. Because use of 126 wheat flour in any drug product is so rare, we do not have good information regarding upper, 127 lower, and typical levels that would be present in a drug product. We believe individuals with 128 celiac disease might choose to avoid oral drug products that are labeled as containing wheat flour 129 in the absence of more detailed information about the drug product’s gluten content. 130

candidates.statement: As with wheat gluten and wheat flour, we believe wheat starch is added to oral drug products as 134 an ingredient only very rarely. Other sources of starch (e.g., corn, potato) are more commonly 135 used in pharmaceutical products. As discussed in section II.B of this guidance, any oral drug 136 product that contains wheat starch as an intentionally added ingredient should be labeled to 137 indicate its presence. 138
candidates.context: A monograph for wheat starch in the National Formulary (NF) includes a 0.3 percent limit on 140 total protein but does not include a limit on gluten content. 7 The gluten content will be some 141 proportion of the total protein content. Based on published information, we understand the gluten 142 content of wheat starch suitable for use in drug products is variable but is typically in the range 143 of 100 to 500 mg/kg (see, e.g., Kasarda, Dupont, et al. 2008). Based on our review of drug 144 formulation information, we expect wheat starch—in the rare cases in which it is used in oral 145 drug products—to contribute less than 0.1 mg gluten to a unit dose of an oral drug product. 146

candidates.statement: Drugs that are licensed biological products (i.e., they are regulated under a biologics license 282 application (BLA)) are subject to additional labeling requirements described in 21 CFR part 610, 283 subpart G. In particular, 21 CFR 610.61 requires identification of certain types of inactive 284 ingredients, including preservatives, “known sensitizing substances,” and “inactive ingredients 285 when a safety factor.” 286
candidates.context: Although not currently mandated by FDA’s regulations, manufacturers of prescription oral drug 278 products generally provide a list of inactive ingredients in the DESCRIPTION section of the 279 prescribing information. 18 We interpret the requirement that inactive ingredients be identified in the labeling of biological 288 products “when a safety factor” as meaning that wheat gluten and wheat flour must be identified 289 by those names if they are present in orally administered biological products. 290

candidates.statement: Consistent with this provision, the established name used in labeling for any wheat-derived 299 ingredient that is the subject of a monograph in an official compendium must be the monograph 300 title, where there is no official name designated pursuant to section 508. For example, wheat 301 starch (not starch ) is the established name by which wheat starch must be identified in drug 302 labeling. However, the more highly processed ingredients discussed in section II.A of this 303 guidance (ingredients derived from starch and ingredients produced by fermentation) do not 304 include a botanical source such as wheat in the established name of the ingredient because the 305 titles of their compendial monographs do not include this designation. 306

If such a product exists, we would expect wheat gluten to 321 be included in its labeled list of inactive ingredients. candidates.statement: We encourage drug manufacturers to have accurate information about their products’ gluten 329 content available so they can respond to questions from consumers and health care professionals. 330 Manufacturers should pay attention to possible sources of gluten in their products, consider 331 specifications when appropriate, and consider the impact of changes in ingredient sources or 332 formulations on gluten content. 333

candidates.statement: We encourage use of this recommended labeling statement to provide health care professionals 354 and consumers with consistent, clear, accurate, and readily understood information about the 355 gluten content of the pharmaceutical products they use. Furthermore, this phrase allows easy 356 searching for terms such as gluten and wheat . This recommended labeling statement does not 357 describe a drug as gluten-free because we have not established criteria for gluten-free statements 358 on oral drug products, and it may be difficult to substantiate that a drug product is free of gluten. 359 We are not aware of analytical test methods currently validated to detect or quantify gluten in 360 finished drug products or in drug ingredients at the low levels at which it would generally be 361 expected to be present, if at all. Furthermore, we have not determined whether a gluten-free 362 statement on an oral drug product should refer to an absence of intact gluten or whether such a 363 statement should also require an absence of gluten peptides. 364

candidates.statement: When used, a voluntary gluten statement should be included in the DESCRIPTION section of 465 the prescribing information. Specifically, it should appear at the end of the inactive ingredients 466 list. If the oral drug product has associated FDA-approved patient labeling, the statement should 467 also appear in that patient labeling, either at the end of an inactive ingredients list or at the end of 468 the patient labeling, after the name and address of the manufacturer, packer, or distributor. In 469 addition, if a voluntary gluten statement is included on the immediate container label and, if 470 applicable, carton labeling, it should appear on the side or back panel. The statement should not 471 appear on the principal display panel, to avoid interference with the required or recommended 472 information that appears on labels and labeling. 35
